hook_text: Watch an empty cooldrink can crush itself flat in a split second. Nobody touches it. What squashes it?
clip_script: Boil a little water in an empty can until it fills with steam. Grab it with tongs and flip it into cold water. Crack, it is flat. Nobody touched it. What did it? Air. Right now billions of billions of air particles are crashing into every surface around you, including your skin, pressing about a kilogram onto every square centimetre at the coast. You do not feel it because your body pushes back equally. In the can, the steam was pushing back too, until the cold water turned it into a few drops. With almost nothing left inside to push outward, the air outside won. That push from colliding particles is gas pressure. Add more particles, heat them up, or squeeze them into less space, and the pressure rises. That is why your tyres get hard, and why an aerosol can must never go in a fire.
visual_style: A whiteboard can over a flame, flipped into a bowl and crushing, then a zoom into particles hitting the outside walls while the inside empties, then quick sketches of a tyre, a straw and an aerosol can.
pacing: A sudden crush, a pause to explain, then quick everyday examples.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and explain gas pressure with particles.
